_meta.descricao: Patriarchs, prophets, kings, women and other figures of the Old and New Testaments, complementing the books in the Bible category.
_meta.aviso: The Twelve Apostles are already covered in the Saints category; this category covers other relevant biblical figures, whether canonized or not.

itens.resumo: The first man and the first woman, according to the biblical account of creation, whose disobedience introduces original sin into humanity.
itens.corpo:
The Book of Genesis narrates the creation of the human being in two complementary accounts. In the first (Gen 1:26-28), God creates "man in his own image" — "male and female he created them" — and entrusts to them dominion over the earth. In the second, which is older from a literary standpoint (Gen 2:4-25), the Lord forms the man (adam, "earthy," from adamah, "earth") from the dust of the ground and breathes into him the "breath of life"; then, seeing that "it is not good that the man should be alone," he forms the woman from one of his ribs, and Adam recognizes her with the first human words recorded in the Bible: "This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh" (Gen 2:23). Both live naked and without shame in the Garden of Eden, in a state of original friendship with God that the Catholic tradition calls "original justice."

The rupture comes in chapter 3: the serpent — read by tradition as a figure of the devil (cf. Wis 2:24; Rev 12:9) — insinuates to Eve doubt about the goodness of the divine command not to eat of the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Eve eats and also gives some to Adam, and "the eyes of both were opened," but not to the divinization promised by the serpent, but rather to shame, fear, and hiding from God. The sentence follows: the serpent is cursed and receives the announcement of the "protoevangelium" — the enmity between its offspring and that of the woman, whose offspring will crush its head (Gen 3:15), read by Christian tradition, since the earliest Fathers, as the first messianic promise, pointing to Christ and to Mary, the "new Eve"; the woman receives the pain of childbirth and subordination to her husband; the man, the toilsome labor of the earth and mortality ("you are dust, and to dust you shall return"). Both are driven out of Eden, and cherubim with a flaming sword guard the way to the tree of life.

Catholic theology, systematized above all by Saint Augustine in his polemic against Pelagius in the 4th-5th centuries, reads in this episode the origin of "original sin": a historical fault of the first parents that wounds human nature at its origin and is transmitted, not by imitation but by generation, to all humanity, depriving it of original grace without, however, totally corrupting nature. The Council of Trent defined this teaching as a dogma of faith in 1546, and the Catechism of the Catholic Church (nos. 396-412) takes it up, explaining that the account in Genesis uses "figurative language," but affirms "a primeval event, a deed that took place at the beginning of the history of man" (CCC 390). Saint Paul had already laid the foundations of this reading by contrasting Adam and Christ: "as sin came into the world through one man and death through sin, [...] so by the obedience of one man many will be made righteous" (Rom 5:12-19); for this reason the liturgy and the Fathers call Christ the "new Adam," who repairs by his obedience the disobedience of the first. The Easter hymn of the Exsultet even sings of the "happy fault" (felix culpa) of Adam, which earned "so great a Redeemer."

In popular iconography and piety, Adam and Eve frequently appear flanking scenes of the crucifixion — the skull at the foot of the cross, according to an ancient tradition, would be that of Adam himself, buried at Golgotha, so that the blood of Christ would symbolically flow over the remains of the first man. Judaism and Islam also revere Adam as the first prophet and father of humanity, though without the Christian doctrine of original sin, which Orthodoxy and Judaism likewise do not share in the same way as the Latin West.
fontes: Vatican News, "The influence of Eve and Mary on women in patristic doctrine"

itens.resumo: Righteous patriarch who, by divine command, builds an ark to save his family and pairs of animals from the Flood.
itens.corpo:
A descendant of Adam through the line of Seth (Gen 5), Noah is presented as "a righteous man, blameless in his generation; Noah walked with God" (Gen 6:9) — the only one deserving of salvation in a humanity that God sees as corrupted by violence (Gen 6:11-13). He then receives the command to build an ark of gopher wood, with three decks, covered with pitch inside and out, to shelter his family — his wife, his three sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth, and their wives — and pairs (seven of each clean species, according to Gen 7:2) of all the animals, while a flood of forty days and forty nights would cover the earth as punishment for human wickedness.

The biblical account of the Flood echoes and at the same time transforms much older traditions from Mesopotamia, such as the Sumerian-Akkadian myth of Utnapishtim, told in the Epic of Gilgamesh, and the Poem of Atrahasis: in both, a hero is warned by a god to build a boat and escape a universal flood. The theological difference is decisive — whereas in the Mesopotamian myths the gods destroy out of caprice or irritation at the noise of men, in Genesis the flood is a moral response to corruption and violence, and God acts with justice, sparing the righteous Noah and renewing all creation through him. After the ark comes to rest on the mountains of Ararat and the waters subside — confirmed by the flight of the raven and, above all, of the dove that returns with an olive branch (Gen 8:11), an image later incorporated into Christian iconography as a symbol of peace and of the Holy Spirit — Noah offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving.

God then establishes with Noah, his descendants, and "every living creature" a universal covenant — the first explicit covenant in the Bible —, promising never again to destroy all flesh by the waters of a flood, and gives the rainbow as the perpetual sign of this promise (Gen 9:8-17). It is also to Noah that the precepts are given which Jewish tradition would later call the "Noahide laws" — the prohibition of shedding human blood and of eating meat with its blood —, understood as the moral minimum required of all humanity, and not only of the chosen people. The rabbinic tradition of the following centuries, reflected in the Talmud and the Midrash, expands the figure of Noah as a "preacher of righteousness" who, during the 120 years of building the ark, supposedly warned his contemporaries in vain to repent.

The Christian tradition, already in texts of the New Testament (1 Pet 3:20-21), read the water of the Flood as a prefiguration of Baptism, which saves "not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a clear conscience"; the ark, in turn, became a patristic symbol of the Church, the only place of salvation amid the shipwreck of sin. The final and less edifying episode of Noah's life is his drunkenness after planting a vineyard and the curse laid upon Canaan, son of Ham, because Ham had mocked his father's nakedness (Gen 9:20-27) — a narrative used, in a tragic and distorted way, centuries later to justify the enslavement of African peoples, a reading now unanimously rejected by Catholic exegesis.

itens.resumo: The first patriarch, father of faith for Jews, Christians and Muslims, called by God to leave his land and receive the promise of a great posterity.
itens.corpo:
Originally from Ur of the Chaldeans, in Lower Mesopotamia, Abram migrates with his father Terah to Haran, in the north, where he receives the call that the Judeo-Christian tradition regards as the founding act of the history of salvation: "Go from your country and your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you" (Gen 12:1). With this command comes a threefold promise: a great posterity, a land, and a blessing that, through him, would reach "all the families of the earth" (Gen 12:2-3). Already old and without children by Sarah, Abram obeys, crosses Canaan, goes down to Egypt in time of famine and returns richer, parting amicably from his nephew Lot, who chooses the region of Sodom.

Throughout Genesis 12-25, his life is marked by episodes that tradition reads as successive trials of faith: the armed rescue of Lot, captured by enemy kings, followed by the enigmatic encounter with Melchizedek, "king of Salem and priest of God Most High," who offers him bread and wine and blesses him, an episode that the New Testament (Heb 7) and the Catholic Eucharistic liturgy read as a prefiguration of the priesthood of Christ; the covenant sealed in a night vision, when God promises Abram descendants "as numerous as the stars of heaven" (Gen 15:5-6), and the text adds the verse that is central to the whole Pauline theology of justification: "he believed the Lord, and he reckoned it to him as righteousness"; and, later, the institution of circumcision as the "sign of the covenant" in the flesh of every male of his descendants (Gen 17), the moment in which God changes his name from Abram ("exalted father") to Abraham ("father of a multitude"), and that of Sarai to Sarah.

From the couple's impatience in the face of barrenness comes the episode of Hagar, Sarah's Egyptian servant, by whom Abraham has Ishmael, recognized by Islamic tradition as the ancestor of the Arabs and of the Prophet Muhammad himself, which makes Abraham a patriarch common to the three Abrahamic religions. Only afterward, at the age of one hundred, does Abraham see the birth of the son of the promise, Isaac, from Sarah. The narrative and theological summit of his life, however, is the so-called Akedah ("binding"): God commands him to sacrifice Isaac himself on Mount Moriah, and Abraham obeys until the last moment, when an angel stays his hand and a lamb is provided for the holocaust in place of his son (Gen 22). Saint Paul (Rom 4) and the Letter to the Hebrews (Heb 11:17-19) see in this episode the supreme model of faith that relies entirely on God "hoping against hope," and the Fathers of the Church associated the only son carrying the wood of his own sacrifice with the figure of Christ carrying the cross.

Abraham dies at the age of 175 and is buried by Isaac and Ishmael in the cave of Machpelah, bought from Ephron the Hittite, the only piece of land he would possess in his lifetime in the promised land (Gen 23; 25:7-10). He is invoked in the Roman Canon of the Mass as father of those who believe, called "our father in faith" by the Catholic liturgy, and Jesus refers to himself as prior to him ("before Abraham was, I am," Jn 8:58), a statement that the evangelists record as a cause of scandal for his Jewish listeners. His figure remains, to this day, the symbolic meeting point between Jews, Christians and Muslims, all claiming to be "children of Abraham" by faith or by flesh.

itens.resumo: Wife of Abraham, who gives birth to Isaac at an advanced age, fulfilling the divine promise of descendants.
itens.corpo:
Half-sister and wife of Abraham, Sarai — her name later changed by God to Sarah, "princess" (Gen 17:15) — accompanies her husband from Ur of the Chaldeans to Canaan, sharing the uncertainties of the whole pilgrimage: on two occasions she is presented by Abraham as his "sister," and not his wife, before foreign rulers (the Pharaoh of Egypt and Abimelech of Gerar), an episode in which her beauty exposes her to the risk of being taken into another man's harem, and from which God delivers her by direct intervention (Gen 12:10-20; 20:1-18).

The central mark of her biblical life is her barrenness lasting for decades — "Sarai was barren; she had no child" (Gen 11:30) —, which leads her, following a legal custom of the ancient Near East well documented in texts from Nuzi and Mari, to give her Egyptian maidservant Hagar to Abraham so that an heir might be born of her; from the resulting son, Ishmael, domestic tensions would arise that would accompany her for the rest of her life. The divine promise that Sarah herself would have a son is received by her, at ninety years of age, with a laugh of disbelief hidden behind the door of the tent — "After I have grown old, and my husband is old, shall I have pleasure?" (Gen 18:12) —, a laugh that God does not let go unnoticed and that gives its name to the son who would be born, Isaac (Yitzchak, "he laughs" or "God laughs/smiles"), a sign that what is humanly impossible becomes possible through divine fidelity.

After the birth of Isaac, Sarah demands that Abraham cast out Hagar and Ishmael so that the slave's son would not share the inheritance with the son of the promise (Gen 21:9-14) — an episode that Saint Paul takes up allegorically in Galatians 4:21-31, contrasting Hagar, a figure of the old covenant and of the slavery of the Law, with Sarah, a figure of the covenant of promise and of the freedom of the children of God through faith, "children of the promise, like Isaac." Sarah dies at the age of 127 in Hebron and is the first to be buried in the cave of Machpelah, purchased by Abraham as the family's first property in the promised land (Gen 23) — a tomb that would also become that of Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, and Leah. The Letter to the Hebrews explicitly includes her in the gallery of the heroes of faith: "By faith Sarah herself [...] received power to conceive, [...] because she considered him faithful who had made the promise" (Heb 11:11), and she is revered to this day as the first of the matriarchs of Israel.

itens.resumo: Son of Abraham and Sarah, spared from sacrifice by divine intervention, father of Esau and Jacob.
itens.corpo:
Second patriarch of Israel, Isaac is the only son whom God had promised to Abraham and Sarah when both were already "advanced in years," born in Beersheba after twenty-five years of waiting since the first promise (Gen 15). His name, Yitzchak ("he laughs"), preserves the memory of his parents' incredulous laughter on hearing the announcement of his birth and, with the fulfillment of the promise, turns into laughter of joy: "God has made laughter for me; every one who hears will laugh over me," says Sarah (Gen 21:6).

Still a boy or young man, he is the protagonist, alongside his father, of the most dramatic episode of his life: taken to Mount Moriah to be offered as a burnt offering by divine command, he himself carries the wood for his own sacrifice and innocently asks where the lamb is — a question answered only at the last moment, when an angel stays Abraham's hand and a ram caught by its horns in a thicket is offered in his place (Gen 22:1-19). Christian tradition, from the earliest Fathers onward, saw in this episode (the Akedah, "binding," in Jewish tradition) a figurative anticipation of the Passion: the only and beloved son who carries the wood of his own death, spared by a substitute lamb, prefiguring the "Lamb of God" who would in fact be sacrificed on Calvary.

As an adult, Isaac does not personally choose his wife: Abraham sends his trusted servant to Mesopotamia, and the servant, guided by a sign asked for in prayer beside a well, recognizes in Rebekah, Abraham's grandniece, the one destined for him — a long and detailed narrative (Gen 24) that commentators point to as one of the most complete accounts in the Bible of divine providence acting through apparently ordinary circumstances. After twenty years of the couple's barrenness, the twins Esau and Jacob are born, already struggling in their mother's womb, foretelling the rivalry that would mark all their descendants (Gen 25:19-26). Isaac repeats, with Rebekah, the same stratagem of his father before a foreign ruler — presenting her as his sister out of fear (Gen 26:6-11) — and prospers as a farmer and herdsman in the region of Gerar, reopening the wells that the Philistines had stopped up after Abraham's death, a gesture read as fidelity to his father's inheritance.

Now old and blind, Isaac is deceived by Rebekah and Jacob, who disguises himself as Esau to receive the paternal blessing meant for the firstborn (Gen 27) — a blessing that, once given, was legally irrevocable, and which the narrative presents with moral ambiguity, not hiding the deceit but recognizing in it the instrument by which God's plan, announced before the twins' birth, is fulfilled. Isaac dies at the age of 180, "old and full of days," and is buried by Esau and Jacob, reconciled, in the cave of Machpelah, beside his parents (Gen 35:27-29). He is the discreet transitional figure between the two great patriarchs Abraham and Jacob, and his life — marked more by silent obedience and by the continuity of the covenant than by great undertakings of his own — was read by patristic tradition, because of his peaceful temperament and his near-sacrifice, as a "type" of Christ, the Prince of Peace.

itens.resumo: Patriarch who, after wrestling with an angel, receives the name "Israel" and becomes the father of the twelve tribes.
itens.corpo:
The younger son of Isaac and Rebekah, Jacob is born clutching the heel of his twin brother Esau — hence his name, traditionally associated with «he who holds the heel» or «supplanter» (Gen 25:26). While still young, he buys Esau's birthright for a dish of lentils, and later, guided by his mother, disguises himself as Esau to obtain from his blind father, Isaac, the solemn blessing meant for the firstborn (Gen 25:29-34; 27:1-40). Once the deceit is discovered, he flees his brother's wrath to Haran, to the house of his uncle Laban, and on the way at Bethel he has the famous vision of a ladder joining earth to heaven, with angels ascending and descending and God himself at the top, renewing for him the promise made to Abraham and Isaac (Gen 28:10-22) — an episode that gives the place its name («Bethel», «house of God») and that Christian tradition associates, from John 1:51 onward, with the figure of Christ as the true link between heaven and earth.

In Haran, Jacob works fourteen years for his two wives, Leah and Rachel, daughters of Laban, who deceives him on the wedding night by substituting the elder sister for the promised bride — a blow that mirrors, almost as poetic justice, the very deception Jacob had inflicted on Esau. From the marriage to Leah and Rachel and their maidservants, Bilhah and Zilpah, are born the twelve sons and the daughter Dinah who would give rise to the twelve tribes of Israel. After twenty years of service, Jacob departs secretly with his family, flocks, and possessions back to Canaan, being reconciled along the way with Laban, who pursues him, and preparing with apprehension to meet Esau again.

On the eve of that reunion, on the bank of the river Jabbok, occurs the most enigmatic episode of his life: alone, Jacob wrestles all night with a «man» whom the text deliberately leaves ambiguous — interpreted by tradition as an angel or a theophany of God himself — and, though wounded in the hip, refuses to let him go without receiving a blessing. He then receives the new name «Israel», explained in the text itself as «one who has striven with God and with men, and has prevailed» (Gen 32:23-33), a name that would come to designate not only the patriarch, but the whole people of his descendants. The reunion with Esau, feared as vengeance, resolves itself in an embrace and tears (Gen 33).

The final years of Jacob's life in Canaan are marked by family tragedies — the rape of Dinah and the bloody vengeance of her brothers at Shechem (Gen 34), the death of Rachel in giving birth to Benjamin, and above all the rivalry among the sons that leads to the sale of Joseph, his favorite, as a slave to Egypt. It is this same Joseph who, years later, now an Egyptian governor, arranges for the whole clan to come to the region of Goshen during the great famine, where Jacob spends the last seventeen years of his life. Before dying, at the age of 147, he pronounces over each of his twelve sons a prophetic oracle (Gen 49) that foretells the destiny of their respective tribes — reserving for Judah the promise of a scepter that would not depart «until he comes to whom it belongs», a text read by Jewish and Christian messianic tradition as a distant announcement of the Messiah. He is buried, at his own wish, in the cave of Machpelah, alongside the other patriarchs (Gen 49:29-33; 50:1-14).

itens.resumo: Son of Jacob, sold by his brothers as a slave, who becomes governor of Egypt and saves his family from famine.
itens.corpo:
The son of Jacob and Rachel, and therefore his father's favorite in his old age, Joseph receives from his father a special tunic — traditionally translated as "of many colors" — which becomes a symbol of the favoritism that arouses the hatred of his ten older brothers, aggravated by two dreams in which Joseph sees himself honored by the whole family (Gen 37:1-11). The brothers at first plan to kill him but, at Judah's suggestion, end up selling him to Ishmaelite/Midianite merchants who take him to Egypt, while they stain his tunic with goat's blood to make Jacob believe that a wild beast had devoured him.

In Egypt, Joseph is bought by Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, and prospers to the point of managing his master's entire household, until he is falsely accused of harassment by Potiphar's wife, whom he had refused out of fidelity to God and to his master — an episode that leads him to prison (Gen 39). In prison, he correctly interprets the dreams of two royal officials imprisoned with him, and this fame reaches Pharaoh when he has disturbing dreams — seven fat cows devoured by seven lean ones, seven full ears of grain devoured by seven withered ones — which no one in Egypt can decipher. Joseph interprets them as a announcement of seven years of great abundance followed by seven years of severe famine, and proposes a storage plan that persuades Pharaoh to raise him, overnight, to governor of all Egypt, second only to the sovereign himself (Gen 41).

When the famine also strikes Canaan, Joseph's brothers go down to Egypt to buy grain and present themselves, without recognizing him, before the very brother they had sold. Joseph tests them before revealing himself, in one of the most emotionally intense moments of the Old Testament, weeping aloud and reassuring them: "it was not you who sent me here, but God [...] to preserve your lives by a great deliverance" (Gen 45:4-8) — a formulation that would become classic in the biblical theology of providence, showing how God weaves good out of evil human intentions ("you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good," Gen 50:20). Jacob and the whole family then settle in the region of Goshen, beginning the Hebrew presence in Egypt that, generations later, would end in the slavery narrated in Exodus.

The patristic tradition saw in Joseph one of the most complete "types" of Christ in the Old Testament: beloved son of the father, rejected and sold by his own brothers, thought to be dead, exalted after unjust humiliations and made, in the end, the savior of those very men who had betrayed him. Authors such as Saint John Chrysostom, Saint Ambrose and Saint Ephrem the Syrian developed this parallel extensively — Ephrem even contrasts Joseph, who "feeds Egypt with material bread," with Jesus, who "nourishes the world with the living bread come down from heaven." Joseph dies in Egypt at the age of 110, but before that he asks that his bones be carried back to the promised land when God would visit his people (Gen 50:24-25) — a promise fulfilled centuries later, during the Exodus (Ex 13:19), and cited by the Letter to the Hebrews as the patriarch's last and discreet act of faith (Heb 11:22).
fontes: A Mensagem, "Did Joseph prefigure Jesus Christ?"

itens.resumo: The greatest leader and lawgiver of the Old Testament, who frees Israel from slavery in Egypt and receives the Law at Sinai.
itens.corpo:
Born into a Levite family at a time when Pharaoh had ordered every newborn Hebrew boy to be killed, Moses is saved as an infant by his mother, who places him in a papyrus basket on the waters of the Nile; taken in by Pharaoh's own daughter, he is raised in the Egyptian court, but, by providential arrangement, is nursed by his own mother (Ex 2:1-10). As an adult, he kills an Egyptian overseer who was beating a Hebrew and flees to Midian, where he marries Zipporah, daughter of the priest Jethro, and lives as a shepherd until the decisive episode of his life: the vision of the bush that burns without being consumed, on Mount Horeb, where God reveals to him his own name, "I Am Who I Am" (YHWH), and sends him back to Egypt to free the enslaved Hebrews (Ex 3).

Faced with Pharaoh's refusal, God sends, through Moses and his brother Aaron, the ten plagues—from the blood of the Nile to the death of the firstborn—which culminate in the institution of the Jewish Passover, celebrated on the last night before the departure, when the blood of the lamb on the doorposts protects the Hebrews from the "destroying angel" (Ex 12). The Exodus proper follows: the crossing of the Sea of Reeds (traditionally the "Red Sea"), with the waters that part and then swallow the pursuing Egyptian army, celebrated in the ancient "Song of the Sea" (Ex 15), one of the most archaic poetic texts of the Hebrew Bible.

In the desert, during forty years of pilgrimage, Moses acts as lawgiver, judge, and intercessor: he goes up Mount Sinai and receives from God the tablets of the Law with the Ten Commandments (Ex 20; Deut 5), as well as an extensive body of ritual, moral, and social precepts that would organize the whole religious and civil life of Israel—the core of what tradition would call the "Law of Moses" or the Torah, the first five books of the Bible, whose direct Mosaic authorship is today qualified by historical-critical exegesis, which recognizes in it later redactional layers, without denying Moses his foundational role as mediator of the covenant. He repeatedly intercedes for a rebellious people—most notably after the episode of the golden calf, when he breaks the tablets in anger and later carves them anew—and faces constant murmuring over hunger, thirst, and fear of the inhabitants of Canaan.

His own fault—striking the rock at Meribah instead of merely speaking to it, a gesture of distrust before the divine command (Num 20:1-13)—costs him the right to enter the promised land. At the age of 120, from the top of Mount Nebo, he gazes upon Canaan from afar before dying, buried by God himself "in a place that no one knows to this day" (Deut 34:1-6). He is revered as the greatest prophet of the Old Testament—"never since has there arisen in Israel a prophet like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face" (Deut 34:10)—and appears alongside Elijah at the Transfiguration of Jesus (Matt 17:1-8), an episode read as recognition that Christ fulfills and surpasses both the Law (represented by Moses) and the Prophets (represented by Elijah). Christian tradition also saw in Moses a "type" of Christ as lawgiver and liberator, and in episodes such as the bronze serpent lifted up in the desert (Num 21:4-9) an explicit prefiguration of the cross, as Jesus himself affirms in John 3:14.

itens.resumo: Brother of Moses and first high priest of Israel, founder of the Levitical priestly line.
itens.corpo:
Son of Amram and Jochebed, of the tribe of Levi, and elder brother of Moses and Miriam, Aaron is appointed by God to accompany Moses before Pharaoh precisely because of his eloquence, making up for the difficulty Moses himself claims to have ("I am slow of speech and of tongue," Ex 4:10) — for this reason the text calls him Moses' "mouth" (Ex 4:16). It is he who wields the staff that turns into a serpent before the Egyptian court and who brings on several of the ten plagues, acting side by side with his brother throughout the whole confrontation with Pharaoh and the departure from Egypt.

At Sinai, Aaron and his sons are consecrated by Moses, by means of an elaborate rite of anointing, sacrifices and specific liturgical vestments (Ex 28-29; Lev 8), as the first priests of Israel, giving rise to the Levitical priestly line — the "Aaronic priesthood" — which would exclusively exercise the functions of worship in the Temple of Jerusalem for more than a millennium, until its destruction in AD 70. To Aaron also fell the formula of the priestly blessing that the priests of Israel would pronounce over the people: "The Lord bless you and keep you [...]" (Num 6:24-26), still used today in Jewish liturgy and echoed in Christian blessings.

His biblical biography is not free from grave faults: while Moses remains on the mountain receiving the Law, Aaron yields to the pressure of the impatient people and makes the golden calf, proclaiming it before the altar as the god who had brought them out of Egypt (Ex 32) — an episode that exposes the frailty of Aaronic leadership in the face of idolatry and which later rabbinic tradition tried, with some effort, to soften. Aaron also joins Miriam in challenging the exclusive authority of Moses, claiming that God spoke through both of them equally (Num 12), an episode resolved by the divine reaffirmation of Moses' unique place as the prophet who sees God "face to face." Later, when the legitimacy of the Aaronic priesthood is challenged by the rebellion of Korah, Dathan and Abiram, God confirms Aaron by causing his rod to blossom miraculously before those of the other tribal leaders, a sign kept in the Ark of the Covenant (Num 17). Like Moses, Aaron also does not enter the promised land because of the disobedience at Meribah, dying on Mount Hor, where his priestly vestments are ritually transferred to his son Eleazar before his death (Num 20:22-29). The Letter to the Hebrews contrasts the priesthood "according to the order of Aaron," limited and hereditary, with the eternal priesthood of Christ "according to the order of Melchizedek" (Heb 7:11-17), reading in Aaron an imperfect and provisional figure of the true High Priest.

itens.resumo: Successor of Moses, who leads Israel in the conquest of the Promised Land.
itens.corpo:
From the tribe of Ephraim, originally called Hoshea, Joshua receives from Moses the new name meaning "the Lord saves" (Num 13:16) — the same Hebrew root as the name "Jesus" in its Greek form. He first appears as Israel's military commander in the victory over the Amalekites in the desert, while Moses, with his arms raised, intercedes on top of a hill (Ex 17:8-13), and from then on he becomes the lawgiver's direct and constant assistant, even accompanying him on the ascent of Sinai. He is one of the twelve spies sent to reconnoiter Canaan and, together with Caleb, the only one to bring back a report confident in the divine promise, against the widespread discouragement of the other ten — a fidelity for which both are spared the punishment that condemns that entire generation to die in the desert without entering the promised land (Num 13-14).

Designated by God, while Moses was still alive, as his successor at the head of the people (Num 27:18-23; Deut 31:7-8), Joshua takes over the leadership after the lawgiver's death and leads the miraculous crossing of the Jordan River, whose waters stop as soon as the priests carrying the Ark of the Covenant step into it — a deliberate echo, in the biblical text, of the crossing of the Red Sea under Moses (Josh 3-4). There follows the military conquest of Canaan, narrated in episodes that became the best known of the book that bears his name: the fall of the walls of Jericho, which collapse after seven days of silent marching by the Israelites around the city and the final blast of the rams' horn trumpets (Josh 6); the initial setback and then the victory at Ai; the covenant with the inhabitants of Gibeon, obtained by their deception; and the battle in which, according to the account, the sun and the moon stand still in the sky at Joshua's request so that Israel might complete the victory by daylight (Josh 10:12-14), a poetic episode cited from the "Book of the Just One," now lost.

Once the conquest of the main regions is complete, Joshua presides over the division of the land among the twelve tribes by lot (Josh 13-21) and, already advanced in age, gathers the people at Shechem for a last solemn exhortation, in which he renews the covenant and pronounces the phrase that would become emblematic of Israel's faith: "as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord" (Josh 24:15). He dies at the age of 110 and is buried in his tribal inheritance, at Timnath-serah, in the hill country of Ephraim (Josh 24:29-30). Christian tradition, noting the coincidence of his name with Jesus and his role of leading the people to the promised land, saw in Joshua a "type" of the one who would lead humanity to the true and definitive rest, a reading already explored by the Letter to the Hebrews (Heb 4:8-9).

itens.resumo: Prophetess and judge of Israel, the only woman among the biblical "judges," who leads the deliverance from Canaanite oppression.
itens.corpo:
In the period of the Judges — about two hundred years, between the conquest of Canaan and the beginning of the monarchy, when Israel was governed by local charismatic leaders without crown or dynasty —, Deborah is the only woman listed among these "judges," and also the only one explicitly described as a prophetess. The text presents her "judging" Israel as she sits under a palm tree, between Ramah and Bethel, in the hill country of Ephraim, where the people came up to consult her in disputes (Judg 4:4-5).

When the Canaanite king Jabin of Hazor and his general Sisera had oppressed Israel for twenty years with nine hundred chariots of iron — military technology far superior to that of the Israelites —, Deborah summons Barak of Naphtali and commands him, in God's name, to gather ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun on Mount Tabor to face the Canaanite army at the river Kishon. Barak hesitates and agrees to go only if Deborah accompanies him; she consents, but announces that, because of this hesitation, the honor of the final victory would not be his, "for the Lord will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman" (Judg 4:8-9). The battle ends in a Canaanite rout, and Sisera flees on foot, seeking refuge in the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite; she welcomes him, gives him milk, and, when he falls asleep exhausted, kills him by driving a tent peg into his temple — fulfilling Deborah's word literally (Judg 4:17-22).

The victory is celebrated in the so-called "Song of Deborah" (Judg 5), attributed to the prophetess herself and to Barak, considered by many exegetes one of the oldest poetic texts preserved in the Hebrew Bible, perhaps contemporary with the very events it describes (12th century B.C.). The song exalts the "arm of the Lord" in the victory, celebrates with admiration the deed of Jael — "most blessed of women be Jael" — and contrasts the joy in Israel with the image, of rare narrative delicacy, of Sisera's mother peering through the window, waiting for a son who would never return. Later Jewish tradition counted Deborah among the seven prophetesses of Israel, and her figure is remembered as a biblical example of legitimate female leadership, political and military as well as spiritual, in a predominantly patriarchal social and religious context.

itens.resumo: Judge of Israel with superhuman strength tied to a Nazirite vow, betrayed by Delilah.
itens.corpo:
A son of Manoah, of the tribe of Dan, Samson has his birth announced by an angel to his mother, until then barren, who receives specific instructions: the son would be a Nazirite "from the womb," consecrated to God by a vow that included never drinking wine or fermented drink, not touching corpses and, above all, never cutting his hair, the visible sign of this consecration (Judg 13). A judge of Israel for twenty years during the period of Philistine domination — the coastal people, technologically superior because they had mastered ironworking, who oppressed the Israelite tribes of the interior — Samson is presented not as a conventional military leader, but as a kind of solitary hero of superhuman strength, moved as much by the "Spirit of the Lord" as by personal impulses and unruly passions.

His exploits include tearing a lion apart with his bare hands on the way to Timnah, where he was courting a Philistine woman; killing thirty men of Ashkelon to pay a riddle wager lost during his own wedding banquet; burning the Philistine crops by tying torches to foxes; and, alone and unarmed, killing a thousand men using only the jawbone of a donkey (Judg 14-15). Once trapped in Gaza, he tears off the gates of the fortified city and carries them to the top of a hill, a gesture that tradition reads as a symbolic demonstration that no Philistine wall could contain him (Judg 16:1-3).

His downfall comes through his passion for Delilah, a woman from the valley of Sorek bribed by the Philistine leaders to discover the secret of his strength. Three times Samson deceives her with false answers, until, pressed by her insistence, he reveals the truth about the Nazirite vow — and Delilah, taking advantage of his sleep, has the seven locks of his hair cut off, causing his strength to drain away together with the sign of the violated consecration (Judg 16:4-20). Captured, blinded and humiliated, he is set to turn the millstone in the Philistine prison, while his hair slowly begins to grow back. In the temple of the god Dagon, displayed as a trophy before thousands of Philistines gathered for a feast, Samson asks God, in a last prayer, to restore his strength "this once," and, bracing himself against the two central pillars of the building, brings it down upon himself and the crowd, killing at the moment of his death more enemies than in all his life (Judg 16:21-31).

Jewish and Christian tradition reads Samson as an ambiguous and tragic figure: endowed with a vocation and a strength that come entirely from God, but repeatedly compromised by his own moral weakness and lack of mastery over his personal appetites — a symbol of how the divine gift can be squandered by human unfaithfulness, and yet redeemed, in the end, by a last gesture of faith and self-surrender.

itens.resumo: Second king of Israel, traditional author of many Psalms, messianic ancestor of Jesus Christ.
itens.corpo:
The youngest of the sons of Jesse of Bethlehem, of the tribe of Judah, David is chosen and anointed in secret by the prophet Samuel, who, contrary to human expectation based on the appearance of the older brothers, is warned by God: "the Lord sees not as man sees; [...] the Lord looks on the heart" (1 Sam 16:7). Still a young shepherd, he becomes famous by accepting the challenge of the Philistine giant Goliath, who for forty days had mocked the Israelite army, and brings him down with a stone from a sling, then beheads him with the giant's own sword (1 Sam 17), an episode that would become a universal symbol of the victory of faith and courage over brute force.

His friendship with Jonathan, son of King Saul, and his growing popular favor arouse Saul's obsessive jealousy, and Saul pursues him for years; David lives as a fugitive, twice deliberately sparing the king's life when he has him at his mercy, refusing to "put forth my hand against the Lord's anointed" (1 Sam 24; 26). After the deaths of Saul and Jonathan in battle against the Philistines on Mount Gilboa, which David mourns in one of the most moving elegies of the Old Testament (2 Sam 1:19-27), he is acclaimed king, first over Judah and, seven years later, over all of united Israel. He conquers Jerusalem from the Jebusites and makes it the political and religious capital of the kingdom, bringing the Ark of the Covenant there in festive procession (2 Sam 5-6).

It is in this context that the prophet Nathan conveys to him the promise that tradition would call the "Davidic Covenant": God refuses to let David build the Temple, reserving that task for his son, but promises to establish forever the house and throne of his descendant (2 Sam 7:12-16), the foundation of all of Israel's later messianic hope, which would await a "son of David" who would reign forever. The king's human frailty, however, appears starkly in the episode with Bathsheba, wife of his officer Uriah the Hittite: David commits adultery with her and, to cover up the resulting pregnancy, orders Uriah to be placed at the front line of the battle, ensuring his death (2 Sam 11). Confronted by Nathan with the parable of the poor man's ewe lamb, David publicly acknowledges his sin, "I have sinned against the Lord", a repentance that tradition associates with Psalm 51 (Miserere), one of the most influential penitential texts in all of Judeo-Christian spirituality.

The last years of his reign are marked by domestic tragedies, the rape of Tamar by Amnon and the vengeance and rebellion of Absalom, which nearly cost him the throne, before he secures the succession of Solomon, son of Bathsheba, with the decisive help of Bathsheba and the prophet Nathan (1 Kings 1). Tradition attributes to David the authorship of a good part of the Psalter, the "Psalms of David", and the Acts of the Apostles explicitly calls him a prophet (Acts 2:29-31), recognizing in his writings messianic anticipations (Ps 2; 16; 22; 110). The four Gospels deliberately trace the genealogy of Jesus back to David, repeatedly calling him "Son of David" (Mt 1:1; 21:9), and Christian tradition, since the Fathers, reads in the whole life of David (shepherd, anointed one, warrior, king and forgiven sinner) a foreshadowing of Christ himself, the true messianic king of the Davidic line.

itens.resumo: Son and successor of David, a king renowned for his wisdom, builder of the first Temple of Jerusalem.
itens.corpo:
The second son of David and Bathsheba, Solomon comes to the throne in the midst of a succession dispute against his older brother Adonijah, resolved in his favor thanks to the intervention of his mother and the prophet Nathan (1 Kings 1). Early in his reign, on a night visit to the sanctuary at Gibeon, he receives from God, in a dream, the offer to ask for whatever he wished; instead of riches, long life, or victory over enemies, Solomon asks for «an understanding heart to judge your people and to distinguish between good and evil» — a request that pleases God so much that he grants him, besides wisdom, also riches and glory unequaled among kings (1 Kings 3:5-14). The most famous proof of this discernment is the «Judgment of Solomon», in which he exposes the true mother of a child disputed by two women by proposing to divide the baby in half, certain that only the genuine mother would draw back to save her child's life (1 Kings 3:16-28).

His forty-year reign, in the tenth century B.C., is remembered as the political and economic peak of the United Kingdom of Israel: he organizes the administration into twelve tax districts, develops international trade — including the famous visit of the queen of Sheba, drawn by the fame of his wisdom and amazed by his court (1 Kings 10:1-13) — and undertakes the greatest architectural work in all of Israel's history, the first Temple of Jerusalem, built with the help of craftsmen and materials supplied by King Hiram of Tyre and consecrated with a lengthy prayer of dedication (1 Kings 5-8). Tradition also attributes to Solomon the authorship of thousands of proverbs and songs (1 Kings 4:32), reflected in the biblical books of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes (Qoheleth), and the Song of Songs, although modern historical-critical exegesis considers that a good part of these texts was composed or compiled in later periods, under the symbolic patronage of his name as patron of Israel's wisdom tradition.

The biblical text, however, does not hide the king's progressive fall: maintaining, according to the account, seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines for political alliances, Solomon «in his old age» lets himself be led astray by his foreign wives to build altars to deities such as Astarte, Milcom, and Chemosh, provoking divine anger (1 Kings 11:1-13). As punishment, it is announced that the kingdom would be divided after his death — which in fact occurs under his son Rehoboam, giving rise to the separate kingdoms of Judah and Israel. Despite this fall, the figure of Solomon remained in biblical memory and later tradition as the supreme archetype of wisdom granted by God, and Jesus cites him in the Gospels when he says that «something greater than Solomon is here» (Mt 12:42), acknowledging his fame, but pointing to something — and Someone — even greater.

itens.resumo: First king of Israel, whose disobedience and jealousy of David mark his reign and his tragic downfall.
itens.corpo:
The son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin, described as a young man of remarkable stature — "from his shoulders upward he was taller than any of the people" (1 Sam 9:2) —, Saul is anointed in secret by the prophet and last judge Samuel, in response to the demand of the people of Israel for a king "like all the nations," a request that Samuel himself interprets as a rejection not of him, but of God himself as Israel's direct king (1 Sam 8:4-9). The public anointing takes place shortly afterward, by lot before all the people gathered at Mizpah, and Saul, despite his stature, is found hiding among the baggage out of shyness (1 Sam 10:20-24) — a detail that commentators read as an early sign of the interior fragility that would mark his entire reign.

His first years as king are marked by military success, above all in the deliverance of the city of Jabesh-gilead from the Ammonite siege, a victory that consolidates his popular recognition (1 Sam 11). The break with God, however, comes through two decisive acts of disobedience: he personally offers a sacrifice before a battle, usurping a function reserved to the priest, out of impatience in waiting for Samuel (1 Sam 13:8-14); and, in the war against the Amalekites, he spares King Agag and the best of the livestock, contrary to the explicit command of total destruction, and then tries to justify himself by claiming he wished to sacrifice the animals to God — a claim to which Samuel replies with the sentence that would become classic: "to obey is better than sacrifice" (1 Sam 15:22). Because of these failings, Samuel announces that the kingdom would be taken from him and given "to a neighbor of yours, who is better than you" — anticipating the secret anointing of David that follows in the next chapter.

From then on, the biblical text describes Saul as tormented by an "evil spirit from the Lord" (1 Sam 16:14), relieved only when the young David played the harp for him — the same David whose growing military and popular renown, after the victory over Goliath, awakens in the king an obsessive jealousy that leads him to try to kill David personally with a spear and then to pursue him for years through the wilderness, even though David twice deliberately spares his life (1 Sam 18-26). In the final chapters, isolated and on the eve of a decisive battle against the Philistines, a desperate Saul, already abandoned by God, seeks out, in disguise, the medium of Endor to summon the spirit of Samuel, who is already dead — an ambiguous episode that yields only the announcement of his imminent defeat and death (1 Sam 28). The next day, wounded in battle on Mount Gilboa and seeing his sons, among them Jonathan, killed at his side, Saul falls upon his own sword so as not to fall alive into the hands of the Philistines (1 Sam 31). David, on hearing the news, does not celebrate, but composes one of the most beautiful elegies of the Old Testament in honor of Saul and Jonathan (2 Sam 1:17-27) — a gesture that tradition reads as a sign of the respect due, in spite of everything, "to the Lord's anointed."

itens.resumo: One of the greatest prophets of Israel, who confronts the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel and is taken up to heaven in a chariot of fire.
itens.corpo:
A native of Tishbe, in Gilead, and presented without any genealogy or narrated childhood — he appears abruptly before King Ahab announcing a drought as divine punishment (1 Kings 17:1) —, Elijah carries out his ministry in the Northern Kingdom during the ninth century B.C., at the height of the religious syncretism promoted by Ahab and above all by his Phoenician wife Jezebel, who had forcibly introduced the worship of the god Baal and had persecuted the prophets of the Lord. Before the great public confrontation, Elijah is miraculously sustained by the brook Cherith, fed by ravens, and then in the house of a widow of Zarephath, whose flour and oil do not run out throughout the whole drought, and whose son he raises from the dead (1 Kings 17).

The central episode of his life is the confrontation on Mount Carmel: before all the people of Israel gathered together, Elijah challenges the 450 prophets of Baal to a decisive test — two altars prepared, each side calling upon its god to send down fire upon the sacrifice. After the prophets of Baal cry out and cut themselves in vain all day long, Elijah, alone, rebuilds the altar of the Lord, drenches it with water three times, and prays briefly; the fire from heaven immediately consumes the offering, the wood, the stones, and even the water around it, leading the people to fall prostrate crying out, "The Lord, he is God!" — and the prophets of Baal are then put to death by the brook Kishon (1 Kings 18:20-40). The supernatural end of the drought follows immediately, with Elijah running ahead of the royal chariot to Jezreel.

Despite this resounding victory, Elijah falls into deep discouragement in the face of the death threat uttered by Jezebel, flees into the desert, and even asks God for his own death before being strengthened by an angel and walking forty days and forty nights to Mount Horeb (Sinai), where he repeats the experience of Moses: not in the strong wind, the earthquake, or the fire, but in a "tiny whispering sound" he recognizes the presence of God (1 Kings 19:11-13), who sends him back to his mission and designates Elisha to him as his successor and disciple. Another striking episode is his courageous denunciation of King Ahab for the indirect murder of Naboth, owner of a vineyard coveted by the king, announcing the downfall of the entire dynasty (1 Kings 21).

At the end of his earthly life, Elijah is taken up alive to heaven in a whirlwind, in a chariot and horses of fire, before Elisha, without experiencing death (2 Kings 2:1-12) — a biblical case comparable only to that of Enoch (Genesis 5:24). Because he did not die, Jewish tradition developed the expectation of his return before the coming of the Messiah, based on Malachi 3:23-24 ("Behold, I will send you Elijah, the prophet, before the day of the LORD comes, the great and terrible day"); hence the Jewish custom of reserving a place for Elijah at the Passover table. The Gospels take up this expectation by identifying John the Baptist as the one who would come "in the spirit and power of Elijah" (Luke 1:17; Matthew 11:14), and Elijah appears in person, alongside Moses, at the Transfiguration of Jesus on Mount Tabor, speaking with him about his imminent departure in Jerusalem (Matthew 17:1-8) — a scene in which the Law (Moses) and the Prophets (Elijah) recognize in Christ their fulfillment.

itens.resumo: Disciple and successor of Elijah, to whom numerous miracles of healing and providence are attributed.
itens.corpo:
The son of Shaphat, a farmer from Abel-meholah, Elisha is called by Elijah, who, following a divine command received at Horeb, finds him plowing with twelve yoke of oxen and throws his own mantle over him—a gesture that seals his prophetic vocation. Elisha immediately sacrifices the oxen and burns the plow as fuel for the farewell banquet, breaking definitively with his former life in order to "follow Elijah and minister to him" (1 Kings 19:19-21). For years he serves as the disciple and assistant of his master, until the moment when the latter is taken up to heaven: asking for a "double portion" of Elijah's prophetic spirit—language that evokes the inheritance right of the firstborn son—Elisha sees his master depart in a chariot of fire and picks up the mantle that falls, with which, striking the waters of the Jordan exactly as Elijah had done, he proves that he has received the succession (2 Kings 2:1-15).

His ministry, which extends for about sixty years under several kings of the Northern Kingdom, is characterized by a number of miracles greater than that of any other biblical prophet, many of them directed at everyday and domestic needs: he purifies the harmful waters of Jericho by throwing salt into a spring (2 Kings 2:19-22); he multiplies the little oil of an indebted widow, enabling her to pay her debts and support her children (2 Kings 4:1-7); he is regularly hosted by a wealthy woman of Shunem, for whom he obtains the birth of a son, despite the advanced age of her husband—a son who later dies suddenly and is raised by him, as he lies upon the child's body until the boy sneezes seven times and opens his eyes again (2 Kings 4:8-37); he multiplies twenty loaves of barley to feed a hundred men, with some left over (2 Kings 4:42-44), an episode read as a prefiguration of Jesus' multiplication of the loaves; and he makes a borrowed iron axe head that had fallen into the Jordan river float, by throwing a piece of wood into the water (2 Kings 6:1-7).

The best-known and theologically weightiest miracle is the healing of the Syrian general Naaman, a leper and commander of an army hostile to Israel, whom Elisha, without even receiving him in person, tells to wash seven times in the Jordan—a command that Naaman obeys only after overcoming his wounded pride, being cleansed and publicly acknowledging that "there is no God in all the earth but in Israel" (2 Kings 5). Elisha refuses any reward for the healing, but his own servant Gehazi, greedy, lies in order to obtain gifts from Naaman in secret and is punished with the leprosy that Naaman had left behind (2 Kings 5:20-27). Elisha also plays a significant political role, anointing Hazael as king of Syria and Jehu as king of Israel (2 Kings 8-9), and dies of illness at an advanced age—but even after his death his prophetic power is manifested: a corpse hastily thrown into his tomb comes back to life upon touching his bones (2 Kings 13:20-21), a final episode that seals his reputation as the prophet of miracles par excellence in the Old Testament.

itens.resumo: One of the greatest prophets of Israel, whose preaching includes some of the Messianic texts most frequently cited by Christianity.
itens.corpo:
The son of Amoz, Isaiah begins his prophetic ministry in Jerusalem "in the year that King Uzziah died" (Is 6:1), around 740 B.C., in a vision of vocation in which he beholds the Lord enthroned in the Temple, surrounded by seraphim who cry out "holy, holy, holy," and he answers the divine call with the words that would become emblematic of every prophetic vocation: "Here am I! Send me" (Is 6:8). His activity extends over some four decades, spanning the reigns of Ahaz and Hezekiah, in a period of successive political crises — the threat of the Syro-Ephraimite coalition, the expansion of the Assyrian Empire over the Northern Kingdom (which falls in 722 B.C.), and the Assyrian siege of Jerusalem under Sennacherib, from which the city escapes almost miraculously (Is 36-37; cf. 2 Kings 18-19).

The figure of Isaiah combines prophetic denunciation of social injustice and cultic hypocrisy — "What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? [...] wash yourselves; make yourselves clean [...] defend the fatherless, plead for the widow" (Is 1:11-17) — with one of the richest Messianic traditions of the entire Old Testament. To him are attributed the oracle of "Immanuel" ("the virgin shall conceive and bear a son," Is 7:14), the announcement of the child who will be called "Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace" (Is 9:6), and the vision of a kingdom of universal peace in which "the wolf shall dwell with the lamb" (Is 11:6) — texts that Christianity, since the Gospels, has read as prophecies directly fulfilled in Jesus (Mt 1:23; Lk 1:32-33).

Modern historical-literary criticism recognizes in the Book of Isaiah, as it has come down to us, at least three major blocks of distinct composition, though gathered under the same name and in a theological unity recognized by tradition: the "Proto-Isaiah" (chapters 1-39), essentially linked to the eighth-century prophet; the "Deutero-Isaiah" or "Book of Consolation" (chapters 40-55), addressed to the exiles in Babylon around 540 B.C., from which come the famous "Servant Songs of the LORD" — four poems about a mysterious figure who suffers and dies for the sins of others, culminating in the fourth and longest of them (Is 52:13–53:12), which describes the Servant as "pierced for our transgressions [...] with his stripes we are healed"; and the "Trito-Isaiah" (chapters 56-66), from the post-exilic period. The New Testament explicitly identifies this Suffering Servant with Jesus Christ (Acts 8:32-35; Mt 8:17; 1 Pet 2:24), and for this reason Isaiah has been called, since Christian antiquity, the "fifth evangelist" — such is the density of his Messianic prophecies. He is also the prophet most frequently cited in the New Testament after the Psalms, and his figure, according to a late Jewish tradition not attested in the Bible, is said to have been sawn in two by order of King Manasseh, a tradition echoed in Hebrews 11:37.

itens.resumo: A prophet who proclaims, amid great personal suffering, the destruction of Jerusalem and the hope of a "new covenant".
itens.corpo:
The son of the priest Hilkiah, of Anathoth, near Jerusalem, Jeremiah is called by God while still young — "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you [...] I appointed you a prophet to the nations" (Jer 1:5) — and reacts with the same reluctance as other biblical prophets, claiming that he does not know how to speak because he is "only a youth"; God responds by touching his mouth and assuring him: "Be not afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you" (Jer 1:6-8). His prophetic activity extends over more than forty years, from the last kings of Judah until the fall of Jerusalem in 587 B.C., one of the most dramatic periods in biblical history.

Throughout this period, Jeremiah insistently proclaims, against the opinion of rival prophets who promised peace and security, that Jerusalem and the Temple would be destroyed because of the people's unfaithfulness, and that submission to Babylon — and not armed resistance — was the only sensible way out in the face of the divine punishment already decreed. This preaching brings him systematic persecution: he is beaten and put in the stocks by the priest Pashhur (Jer 20:1-2), thrown into a muddy cistern where he nearly dies buried in the mire (Jer 38:1-13), accused of treason for advising surrender, and his own scroll of prophecies is cut into pieces and burned by King Jehoiakim (Jer 36). Even so, in a symbolic gesture of hope during the final siege of the city, he buys a field in Anathoth at God's command, signaling that "houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land" after the exile (Jer 32).

Jeremiah is also the author of a collection unique in the Old Testament — the so-called "Confessions" (Jer 11-20), autobiographical passages of personal lament in which the prophet lays before God his anguish, his isolation, and even his anger at having been called to a mission of suffering, going so far as to curse the day of his birth (Jer 20:14-18) — which earned him the traditional epithet of the "weeping prophet." Tradition also attributes to him the Book of Lamentations, five funeral poems on the destruction of Jerusalem, although Jeremiah's authorship of this book is now debated by modern exegesis; and his faithful scribe, Baruch, son of Neriah, records and preserves his oracles, becoming a figure with a book of his own in the broader biblical tradition (the Book of Baruch, found in the Catholic canon).

Despite the predominantly somber tone, it is precisely Jeremiah who conveys one of the most decisive promises of all Scripture for later Christian theology: the announcement of a "new covenant" that God would make with the house of Israel, not like the old one, written on tablets of stone, but engraved directly on the human heart, with definitive forgiveness of sins and direct knowledge of God, "from the least of them to the greatest" (Jer 31:31-34). The New Testament takes up this promise as fulfilled in the person and work of Christ — the words of the institution of the Eucharist, "This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood" (Lk 22:20), directly echo Jeremiah's oracle — and the Letter to the Hebrews quotes it at length as the foundation of the superiority of the Christian priesthood and covenant (Heb 8:8-12). After the fall of Jerusalem, Jeremiah is taken by force to Egypt by a group of fugitive Jews, and there, according to tradition, he ends his days.

itens.resumo: A young Jew exiled in Babylon, renowned for his fidelity and for the apocalyptic visions that bear his name.
itens.corpo:
Of noble or royal lineage from Judah, Daniel was taken as a young man to Babylon among the first exiles, around 605 B.C., when Nebuchadnezzar II subdued Jerusalem, and was chosen, together with other young Jews, to serve in the royal court after training in Chaldean language and literature. There he received the Babylonian name Belteshazzar, but he refused, together with his three companions Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah (better known by their Babylonian names, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego), to defile himself with the food and wine of the royal table, asking permission to eat only vegetables and drink only water — an episode of fidelity to the Jewish dietary laws with which the book opens (Dn 1).

The first half of the book (chapters 1-6) recounts court episodes that became the best known in the biblical tradition: Daniel interprets Nebuchadnezzar's disturbing dream of a statue made of metals decreasing in nobility — gold, silver, bronze, iron, and clay — destroyed by a stone "cut out, not by human hands," a symbolic announcement of the succession of the great world empires (traditionally identified as Babylon, Media-Persia, Greece, and Rome) until the definitive establishment of the kingdom of God (Dn 2); his three companions are thrown into a fiery furnace for refusing to worship a golden statue set up by the king, and they come out unharmed, accompanied by a fourth figure "like a son of the gods" (Dn 3); Daniel deciphers the mysterious inscription "Mene, Mene, Tekel, and Parsin" that appears on the wall during Belshazzar's banquet, announcing the imminent fall of the Babylonian empire (Dn 5); and, already under Medo-Persian rule, he is thrown into the lions' den for continuing to pray publicly to God three times a day, defying a royal decree that forbade any prayer addressed to anyone other than the king himself — and he is found unharmed the next morning, protected by an angel who "shut the lions' mouths" (Dn 6).

The second half of the book (chapters 7-12) changes literary genre, becoming one of the most influential apocalyptic texts of the Old Testament: Daniel has night visions of four beasts symbolizing the same successive empires as the statue of Nebuchadnezzar, culminating in the vision of the "Son of Man" who receives from the "Ancient of Days" an everlasting and universal dominion (Dn 7:13-14) — an image that Jesus repeatedly takes up for himself in the Gospels as his preferred messianic title. The book also contains, in the Greek sections preserved in the Catholic tradition (Septuagint and Vulgate), the episodes of Susanna (the woman unjustly accused, saved by the shrewdness of the young Daniel) and of Bel and the Dragon, which expose the fraud of the idolatrous Babylonian cults. Written in its final form probably in the 2nd century B.C., during the persecution by the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the Book of Daniel served as literature of resistance and hope for faithful Jews under oppression, and its central figure became, in both the Jewish and the Christian traditions, the greatest symbol of unshakable fidelity to God in the face of hostile political power.

itens.resumo: A righteous man who suffers terrible losses and questions the meaning of undeserved suffering, without losing his faith in God.
itens.corpo:
Set in the land of Uz, outside Israel, and presented from the very first sentence as "blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned away from evil" (Job 1:1), Job is described as a rich and blessed man: ten children, thousands of animals, "the greatest of all the people of the East." The book opens with a prose prologue of an almost theatrical tone: in a heavenly assembly, "the satan" (the "accuser," a figure not yet fully identified with the devil of later tradition) challenges God to allow Job's fidelity to be tested through the loss of everything he possesses: goods, children and, finally, his own health, with leprosy or a malignant ulcer "from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head" (Job 1-2). Even so, Job does not curse God, though neither does he hide his pain: "The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord" (Job 1:21).

The central body of the book, an extensive poem that takes up most of its 42 chapters, narrates the visit of three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, who at first sit in silence with Job for seven days, but then engage him in three cycles of poetic speeches on the cause of his suffering. The friends defend, with variations, the so-called theology of retribution then dominant: if Job suffers so much, he must have sinned gravely, since God rewards the just and punishes the wicked. This position is upheld with particular insistence by Eliphaz, who even appeals to a night vision to ground his certainty that "no innocent person ever perished" (Job 4:7). Job firmly rejects this explanation, proclaims his own innocence and challenges God to explain Himself directly, even expressing, amid his anguish, flashes of extraordinary hope, such as the famous confession "I know that my Redeemer lives" (Job 19:25). A fourth interlocutor, the young Elihu, then intervenes with a speech of his own before God's final answer.

The theological climax of the book comes in chapters 38-41, when God finally answers Job, not with a rational explanation of suffering, but "out of the whirlwind," with a series of rhetorical questions about creation ("Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?") that reveal to Job the disproportion between human wisdom and the unfathomable mystery of divine governance over the universe. Job yields, not convinced by arguments, but transformed by the direct encounter: "I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you" (Job 42:5), and he acknowledges having spoken "of things I did not understand." In the prose epilogue, God rebukes the three friends for not having spoken rightly about Him, unlike Job, and restores his fortunes, giving him twice what he had before (Job 42:7-17).

The Book of Job holds a unique place in biblical wisdom literature because it refuses the simple equation between suffering and personal sin, anticipating a question that would run through the whole Judeo-Christian tradition about the meaning of innocent suffering. The Catholic tradition, without offering a closed philosophical answer to the problem of evil, read in Job's trusting surrender an anticipation of Christian faith, and his patience became proverbial, hence the expression "the patience of Job," and the book is read liturgically above all in contexts of mourning and in the funeral liturgy.

itens.resumo: Forerunner of Jesus, son of Elizabeth and Zechariah, who preaches conversion and baptizes in the Jordan (see also the Saints category).
itens.corpo:
Already treated in more detail in the Saints category, John the Baptist deserves a specific entry here as a key figure of the biblical narrative that links the two Testaments. The son of the priest Zechariah and of Elizabeth, both already advanced in years and until then barren, his birth is announced to his father by the angel Gabriel in the sanctuary of the Temple; Zechariah's disbelief at the news costs him his speech until the day of his son's circumcision, when he confirms in writing the name given by the angel — "John," "God is gracious" — and recovers his speech by singing the canticle of the Benedictus (Lk 1:5-25, 57-80). Even in his mother's womb, John already recognizes the presence of Jesus, himself also conceived, "leaping for joy" when Mary visits Elizabeth in the episode of the Visitation (Lk 1:39-45).

As an adult, he withdraws to the desert of Judea, where he lives on locusts and wild honey, clothed in camel's hair — a figure whom the Gospels deliberately associate with the prophet Elijah and with the voice "crying out in the desert: prepare the way of the Lord" announced by Isaiah (Is 40:3; Mk 1:2-3). His preaching calls for radical conversion, a baptism of repentance in the river Jordan, and an unsparing denunciation of religious hypocrisy and social injustice, drawing crowds from all over Judea. When Jesus presents himself to be baptized by him, John at first resists, acknowledging his own littleness before him ("I need to be baptized by you"), and at the moment of the baptism the heavens open, the Spirit descends like a dove, and a voice from heaven proclaims Jesus the beloved Son (Mt 3:13-17). It is also John who, seeing him pass by, publicly identifies him as "the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world" (Jn 1:29, 36), a title that the Catholic liturgy repeats at every Eucharistic celebration before communion.

His prophetic frankness leads to his imprisonment: he publicly denounces the union between the tetrarch Herod Antipas and Herodias, wife of his half-brother Philip, as contrary to the Jewish Law, and Herodias, wounded, plots his death. It is during a birthday banquet of Herod that the daughter of Herodias (traditionally called Salome, although the name does not appear in the Gospels) dances and pleases the tetrarch so much that he promises her, under oath, whatever she might ask; instructed by her mother, she asks for the head of John the Baptist on a platter, and Herod, embarrassed before his guests, orders the beheading (Mt 14:1-12; Mk 6:14-29). Patristic tradition saw in John not only the "last prophet" of the old covenant, but the "forerunner even in death," anticipating by martyrdom the fate that awaited Christ himself. He is venerated as the greatest among those born of women, according to the very words of Jesus (Mt 11:11).

itens.resumo: King of Judea under Roman rule at the time of the birth of Jesus, responsible, according to Matthew, for the massacre of the Holy Innocents.
itens.corpo:
The son of Antipater, an Idumean noble converted to Judaism, Herod rose to the throne of Judea by appointment of the Roman Senate in 40 B.C. and consolidated his power in fact only a few years later, governing as a client king of Rome until his death in 4 B.C. — probably shortly after the birth of Jesus, which places that event historically before the conventional date of the Christian calendar. He is extensively documented by the Jewish historian Flavius Josephus (Antiquities of the Jews and The Jewish War), who portrays him as a skilled and efficient ruler, but also extremely cruel and paranoid about any threat to his power — he even had three of his own sons and one of his wives, Mariamne, executed on suspicion of conspiracy, leading the Emperor Augustus to remark, according to tradition, that it was "safer to be Herod's pig than his son" (a pun between the Greek words hys, pig, and hyios, son, also alluding to his Jewish observance of not eating pork).

His reign is remembered historically for an extraordinary program of public works: he rebuilt the Second Temple of Jerusalem on a grand scale, enlarging the Temple Mount with the monumental platform whose retaining walls — among them the present-day Western Wall — survive to this day; he built the artificial harbor and the city of Caesarea Maritima; he fortified the fortress-palace of Masada, in the Judean desert, as a personal refuge; and he built the Herodium, where he was buried. These works made him one of the most visibly striking figures in the landscape of the Holy Land to this day.

In the Gospel account, Herod appears in the episode of the visit of the Magi from the East, who arrive in Jerusalem asking about the newborn "king of the Jews," guided by a star; troubled by the news and fearing a rival to the throne, Herod pretends that he also wishes to worship the child, but, warned in a dream, the Magi do not return to him, and the king, "in a furious rage," orders the death of all the boys in Bethlehem and its vicinity who were two years old and under — an episode that Matthew reads as the fulfillment of a prophecy of Jeremiah about the weeping of Rachel (Mt 2:1-18). There is no independent record of this massacre in Josephus or in other contemporary sources, which leads some historians to treat it with caution regarding its strict historicity; even so, the episode is fully consistent with Herod's violent and paranoid character, widely documented by other sources, and the Church celebrates the victims as the Holy Innocents, the first martyrs of the Christian era, even if involuntary ones.

itens.resumo: Son of Herod the Great, tetrarch of Galilee and Perea between 4 B.C. and A.D. 39; he ordered the death of John the Baptist and questioned Jesus during the Passion.
itens.corpo:
Herod Antipas was the son of Herod the Great and his wife Malthace, and a full brother of Archelaus. Educated in Rome together with his brothers, he received by his father's will, with the confirmation of the Emperor Augustus, the tetrarchy of Galilee and Perea — "tetrarch" literally means "ruler of a fourth part" —, an office he held from about 4 B.C. until A.D. 39. He therefore governed throughout the entire public ministry of Jesus, and the New Testament calls him both "Herod the tetrarch" and "King Herod."

His historical memory is above all tied to the death of John the Baptist. The Synoptic Gospels relate that the Baptist publicly rebuked his unlawful union with Herodias, the wife of his half-brother Philip, and that the tetrarch had him arrested. Mark 6:14-29 gives the account according to which, during a banquet, the daughter of Herodias — Salome, in tradition — danced and pleased Herod, who promised her under oath whatever she might ask; prompted by her mother, she asked for the head of the Baptist, and the tetrarch, constrained by the promise made before the guests, ordered him beheaded in prison. The Jewish historian Flavius Josephus, in Antiquities of the Jews 18.116-119, confirms the execution of John by order of Antipas, placing the imprisonment and death in the fortress of Machaerus, near the Dead Sea, and explaining the event by the Baptist's popularity among the people.

Beyond the conflict with John, his marriage to Herodias added a personal grievance to the old territorial disputes with Aretas IV, king of the Nabateans and father of his first wife, whom he had repudiated. This conflict led to a war that proved disastrous for Antipas, with Arab victories around A.D. 36 — an episode that, according to Josephus, the people regarded as divine punishment for the death of the Baptist. Antipas was also the founder of Tiberias, a city built on the shores of the Sea of Galilee and named in honor of the Emperor Tiberius.

In the Gospels, he also appears in the trial of Jesus. Luke 23:6-12 tells that Pilate, on learning that Jesus was a Galilean and was therefore under Antipas' jurisdiction, sent him to the tetrarch, who was in Jerusalem for the feast. Herod, who had long wished to see him and hoped to see him perform some miracle, questioned him at length, but Jesus answered him nothing; mocked and clothed in a splendid robe, he was sent back to Pilate, and the two rulers, previously enemies, became friends that day. In Luke 13:32, Jesus refers to him with contempt as "that fox."

His end was deposition. In A.D. 39, urged on by Herodias, he denounced his nephew Agrippa I for conspiracy against the Emperor Caligula; Agrippa, however, a personal friend of Caligula, turned the accusation around. The emperor confiscated Antipas' territories and treasury and exiled him to Gaul — Josephus mentions Lugdunum, and two French cities contend to have been the place, Lyon and Saint-Bertrand-de-Comminges. Herodias accompanied him into exile, where he died. The historian Cassius Dio (59.8) suggests that Caligula had him put to death. His domains were annexed to the tetrarchy of Agrippa I.
