itens.resumo: Roman prefect of Judea who, although he recognizes the innocence of Jesus, authorizes his crucifixion under pressure from the crowd.
itens.corpo: Roman prefect of Judea from AD 26 to 36, Pontius Pilate presides over the Roman trial of Jesus, publicly declaring that he finds no guilt in him, but yielding, under pressure from the crowd and fear of an uprising, to the sentence of crucifixion — an episode recorded to this day in the Creed ("suffered under Pontius Pilate"), historically fixing the moment of the Passion.

itens.resumo: One of the Twelve Apostles who betrays Jesus for thirty pieces of silver, handing him over to the authorities in Gethsemane.
itens.corpo: Treasurer of the apostolic group, Judas Iscariot agrees to hand Jesus over to the religious authorities for thirty pieces of silver, identifying him with a kiss in Gethsemane. According to Matthew, filled with remorse, he returns the money and takes his own life before the crucifixion (Mt 27:3-5); the Acts of the Apostles relates a slightly different version of his death (Acts 1:18-19).

itens.resumo: A Pharisee and member of the Sanhedrin who visits Jesus by night and later takes part, with Joseph of Arimathea, in His burial.
itens.corpo: A Pharisee and member of the Sanhedrin, Nicodemus seeks out Jesus discreetly at night, fearing the reaction of his peers, and receives the teaching on the necessity of being "born again" (Jn 3:1-21). He appears again later, timidly defending Jesus' right to a fair trial, and, in the end, helps Joseph of Arimathea prepare and bury the body of Jesus after the crucifixion.

itens.resumo: A wealthy and influential member of the Sanhedrin who, as a secret disciple of Jesus, asks Pilate for the body of the Crucified One and buries him in his own new tomb, hewn out of the rock.
itens.corpo:
Joseph of Arimathea appears in all four Gospels as a rich man of standing, a member of the Sanhedrin — the supreme council of Jerusalem — who, according to Luke 23:51, had not consented to the decision and action of the other council members against Jesus. Mark 15:43 and Luke 23:50-51 describe him as a "respected member of the council" who was awaiting the Kingdom of God; Matthew 27:57 adds that he was rich. His name derives from Arimathea, a town that many scholars identify with present-day Rantis, in the West Bank, or with the Ramah of Ephraim mentioned in the Old Testament.

The central episode of his life is the burial of Jesus. John 19:38 presents him as a disciple of Jesus, "but secretly, for fear of the Jews": it is he who, after the crucifixion, has the courage to ask Pilate for the Master's body. Pilate grants the request, which was only possible for someone of recognized social standing — the right to bury an executed person depended on the governor's authorization. With him comes Nicodemus, a Pharisee and "ruler of the Jews," who brings about a hundred pounds (about thirty kilograms) of a mixture of myrrh and aloes (Jn 19:39). The two wrap the body in linen cloths with spices, according to the Jewish custom of preparing for burial, and lay it in a new tomb, hewn out of the rock, which Joseph owned near Golgotha (Mt 27:57-60; Mk 15:42-46; Lk 23:50-53; Jn 19:38-42). Since a body was meant to be buried in one's own native land, some authors find it odd that Joseph had a tomb in Jerusalem — an indication that he also lived there or held property there.

Later Christian tradition greatly developed his figure. The Acts of Pilate, also called the Gospel of Nicodemus (an apocryphal text whose core goes back to the second century, already mentioned by Saint Justin), make Joseph the protagonist of the events following the crucifixion, narrating the conflicts between him and the Temple authorities for having buried Jesus. Medieval homilies and accounts, for their part, associated him with the tin trade and with the arrival of Christianity in Britain, linking him to the Arthurian cycle of Glastonbury and to the theme of the Holy Grail. Such traditions, although widely spread in literature and art, have no basis in the canonical texts and are regarded by historical criticism as legendary.

The Catholic Church celebrates his memorial together with that of Saint Nicodemus on August 31, according to the Roman Martyrology, honoring precisely the two "secret disciples" who, in the darkest moment of the Passion, made their adherence to Christ public by giving his body a dignified burial. In art, the episode of the burial, with Joseph and Nicodemus holding the body of Jesus, became a frequent theme, a notable example of which is the Lamentation scene attributed to Giotto in the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua.

itens.resumo: A wealthy, short-statured tax collector who, upon climbing a tree to see Jesus, is converted by an unexpected invitation to host him.
itens.corpo: Chief of the tax collectors in Jericho — a profession despised for collaborating with the Roman occupation — Zacchaeus climbs a sycamore tree in order to see Jesus over the crowd, because of his short stature. Surprised by Jesus, who announces that he will stay at his house that very day, he is converted publicly, promising to restore fourfold to anyone he had wronged.

itens.titulo: The Woman of Samaria at the Well
itens.resumo: A Samaritan woman who converses with Jesus at Jacob's well and becomes one of the first evangelizers recorded in the Gospels.
itens.corpo: In the famous dialogue at the well of Sychar, Jesus reveals to a Samaritan woman — whose ethnicity and personal life made her doubly marginalized — that he is the "living water" and the very Messiah who was expected, in one of the richest theological discourses of the Gospel of John. She runs to announce the encounter to her town, becoming one of the first "evangelizers" recorded in the New Testament.

itens.resumo: Cousin of Mary and mother of John the Baptist, whom she conceives in her old age despite being barren, according to Luke's account.
itens.corpo: Wife of the priest Zechariah, Elizabeth conceives John the Baptist at an advanced age and after long barrenness, as announced by the angel Gabriel to her husband. It is Elizabeth whom Mary visits right after the Annunciation—the episode of the Visitation—and it is she who first recognizes, while still pregnant, the presence of the Messiah in Mary's womb ("Blessed are you among women").

itens.resumo: Two righteous elders who recognize in Jesus, still a child, the Messiah awaited by Israel, in the episode of the Presentation in the Temple.
itens.corpo: In the Temple of Jerusalem, the elder Simeon — to whom it had been revealed that he would not die before seeing the Messiah — recognizes Jesus and sings the canticle "Nunc Dimittis" ("Lord, now you let your servant go in peace"). The prophetess Anna, an elderly widow who lived in the Temple in fasting and prayer, also recognizes the child and begins to speak of him to all who were awaiting the redemption of Jerusalem.

itens.resumo: A prisoner released by the crowd in place of Jesus, in the episode of the Passover custom of releasing one prisoner.
itens.corpo: Described as an insurrectionist or murderer imprisoned for sedition, Barabbas is the prisoner whom the crowd chooses to release instead of Jesus, when Pilate offers them the choice between the two, following a Passover custom of granting amnesty to one prisoner — an episode that Christian tradition reads with strong symbolic weight regarding the human choice between violence and innocence.

itens.resumo: Sisters of Lazarus and hostesses of Jesus in Bethany, a village near Jerusalem; each represents a distinct and complementary way of welcoming and following the Master.
itens.corpo:
Mary and Martha of Bethany are presented in the Gospels as the sisters of Lazarus and inhabitants of the village of Bethany, situated on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, a few kilometers from Jerusalem, on the road that descends to Jericho (Mk 11:1; Lk 19:29). In the Gospel accounts, the home of the two sisters serves as a place of rest and welcome for Jesus in the days leading up to the Passion, and the Fourth Gospel explicitly records that "Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus" (Jn 11:5).

The Gospels attribute three distinct scenes to the Bethany circle. The first is the domestic episode narrated in Luke 10:38-42: while Martha is busy and distracted with the serving at table, Mary sits at the Lord's feet to listen to him. To Martha's complaint — "Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone?" — Jesus replies that Mary has chosen "the better part, which will not be taken away from her." In the spiritual tradition, the passage became the classic contrast between the active life and the contemplative life. The second is the account of the raising of Lazarus (Jn 11), in which the two sisters, at different moments, go out to meet Jesus and express the same grief and the same confession of faith: Martha makes the great declaration "Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God" (Jn 11:27). The third scene is the anointing at Bethany, shortly before the Passion, when Mary anoints the feet of Jesus with costly perfume and wipes them with her hair (Jn 12:1-11); the Fourth Gospel interprets the gesture as an anticipation of the burial, while in the Synoptics the same scene appears in a different setting. Exegetical criticism observes that John reworks the Synoptic tradition of the anointing, giving it a markedly Christological meaning.

The figure of Martha is linked to a well-defined later hagiographical tradition. The name "Martha" transliterates the Greek Μαρθα, in turn derived from the Aramaic מַרְתָּא, meaning "lady" or "mistress." According to the Golden Legend and ancient traditions of southern France, after the dispersion of the first disciples the three siblings of Bethany went to preach in Gaul, and Martha is venerated as the evangelizer of Tarascon, where tradition places her tomb; in the East, another tradition has her die in Larnaca, in Cyprus. She is invoked as patroness of cooks, innkeepers, domestic workers, and housewives.

In the liturgical calendar, the memorial of Saint Martha was celebrated on its own on July 29. On February 2, 2021, Pope Francis determined, through the Congregation for Divine Worship and the Discipline of the Sacraments, that on the same date the three siblings of Bethany — Martha, Mary, and Lazarus — would be remembered together, recognizing in them the witness of hospitality and of friendship with Christ. In the East, Saint Martha is remembered on June 4.

itens.resumo: Friend of Jesus, who was raised by him from the dead four days after burial, in the greatest miracle recounted in the Gospel of John.
itens.corpo: Brother of Martha and Mary of Bethany, Lazarus dies and has already been in the tomb for four days when Jesus, deeply moved ("Jesus wept," Jn 11:35, the shortest verse in the Bible), calls him back to life before a crowd — the last and greatest of the "signs" recounted in the Gospel of John, decisive in intensifying the opposition of the religious authorities against Jesus.

itens.resumo: A Moabite woman who, out of fidelity to her mother-in-law Naomi and to the God of Israel, becomes the great-grandmother of King David and appears in the genealogy of Jesus.
itens.corpo:
A young widow and a foreigner from Moab, Ruth refuses to abandon her mother-in-law Naomi when Naomi decides to return to Bethlehem after the death of her husband and sons, saying to her the words that would become classic: "Where you go I will go, [...] your people shall be my people, and your God my God" (Ruth 1:16). Once in Bethlehem, Ruth gleans ears of grain behind the reapers in the field of Boaz, a relative of Naomi, who welcomes her with kindness and, following the custom of family redemption (levirate), ends up marrying her (Ruth 2-4).

From the marriage of Ruth and Boaz is born Obed, the grandfather of David (Ruth 4:17), so that a Moabite foreigner enters the direct line of the greatest king of Israel — and, through her, the very genealogy of Jesus, which Matthew expressly records (Mt 1:5). The short Book of Ruth is therefore read as a prophetic sign of the opening of God's plan to the Gentiles long before the apostolic preaching, and as one of the most delicate biblical portraits of loyalty, honest work, and divine providence in everyday life.

itens.resumo: A young Jewish woman who becomes queen of Persia and risks her own life to save her people from the extermination planned by the minister Haman.
itens.corpo:
An orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai, Esther is chosen queen of the Persian empire by King Ahasuerus without his knowing of her Jewish origin (Esther 2:7-17). When the powerful minister Haman, offended that Mordecai refused to bow down before him, obtains from the king a decree to exterminate all the Jews in the kingdom, Mordecai asks Esther to intercede, warning her that perhaps she has come to the royal position "for such a time as this" (Esther 4:14).

After fasting with her people, Esther presents herself to the king without being summoned — a gesture that could have cost her her life — and, at two carefully prepared banquets, denounces Haman's plan, and he ends up executed on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai (Esther 5-7). Since the original decree could not be revoked, a new edict allows the Jews to defend themselves, and the victory is celebrated to this day in the Jewish feast of Purim (Esther 9). The Book of Esther is the only book of the Hebrew Old Testament that does not directly mention the name of God, but his providence is read in every turn of the narrative.

itens.resumo: A prophet who flees from his mission to preach in Nineveh, is swallowed by a great fish, and, after repenting, sees the enemy city convert.
itens.corpo:
Sent by God to proclaim conversion to the great city of Nineveh, capital of the dreaded Assyrian Empire, Jonah flees in the opposite direction, boarding a ship for Tarshish. During the voyage, a storm threatens the ship; cast into the sea by lot, he is swallowed by a "great fish" (the Hebrew text says "dag gadol," not specifically a whale), in whose belly he spends three days and three nights until he repents and is returned to dry land (Jon 1-2).

This time Jonah obeys and preaches in Nineveh, which converts entirely, from the king to the last inhabitant, with fasting and penance — to the displeasure of the prophet himself, who preferred to see the enemy city punished rather than pardoned (Jon 3-4). The book ends with a question from God to Jonah about his lack of compassion, leaving his answer open. Jesus cites the "sign of Jonah" — the three days in the belly of the fish — as an anticipated figure of his own death and resurrection (Mt 12:39-40).

itens.resumo: Prophet and priest who carried out his ministry among the Jews exiled in Babylon, proclaiming judgment and, later, the restoration of Israel.
itens.corpo:
A priest taken into exile along with other Jews in the first deportation to Babylon, Ezekiel received his prophetic call around 593 BC, in an impressive vision of the throne of God upon a chariot of winged creatures (Ezek 1). Before the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, he proclaimed, through dramatic symbolic gestures — such as lying for many days on one side or cutting and burning his own hair — the imminent punishment upon the unfaithful city (Ezek 4-5).

After the destruction of the temple, the tone of his preaching changes to hope: his is the famous vision of the valley of dry bones, which come together, receive flesh, and are revived by the breath of God, an image of the future restoration of Israel (Ezek 37:1-14). Ezekiel also describes in detail a rebuilt eschatological temple (Ezek 40-48) and develops the image of the "heart of flesh" that God will give to his people in place of the "heart of stone" (Ezek 36:26), a text read by the Christian tradition as a proclamation of the interior renewal brought by grace.

itens.resumo: Wife of Isaac and mother of the twins Jacob and Esau, chosen by a sign at a well to continue the line of the covenant.
itens.corpo:
Grandniece of Abraham, Rebekah is chosen as Isaac's wife after Abraham's servant, sent to the patriarch's native land, asks God for a sign: that the young woman who offered water to him and to his camels would be the one destined for Isaac. Rebekah fulfills exactly this sign at the well, and agrees to leave at once to marry Isaac, whom she had never seen (Gen 24).

After years of barrenness, Rebekah gives birth to twins who already struggle in her womb—Esau and Jacob—concerning whom she receives the oracle that "the elder shall serve the younger" (Gen 25:21-23). It is Rebekah who, later on, guides and helps Jacob, her favorite son, to obtain by deceit the paternal blessing intended for the firstborn Esau (Gen 27), a decisive episode—though morally ambiguous—for the promise of the covenant to pass through Jacob, the future Israel.

itens.resumo: Jacob's most beloved wife and mother of Joseph and Benjamin, for whom Jacob worked fourteen years in the service of her father Laban.
itens.corpo:
The younger daughter of Laban and cousin of Jacob, Rachel is described as "beautiful and lovely" (Gen 29:17), and Jacob agrees to work seven years for her father in order to marry her. On the wedding night, however, Laban substitutes her older sister, Leah, for the bride, obliging Jacob to work another seven years in order finally to marry Rachel as well (Gen 29:15-30).

While Leah gives birth to several sons, Rachel remains barren for a long time, until God "remembered her" and she conceives Joseph (Gen 30:22-24), who would become a central figure in the history of salvation by preserving his brothers in Egypt. Years later, Rachel dies giving birth to her second son, Benjamin, and is buried near Bethlehem (Gen 35:16-20) — a place venerated to this day as Rachel's Tomb. Her figure is poignantly evoked by the prophet Jeremiah, and the Gospel of Matthew cites that same passage in connection with the massacre of the innocents ordered by Herod: "A voice was heard in Ramah [...]: it was Rachel weeping for her children" (Matt 2:18; cf. Jer 31:15).

itens.resumo: Wife of Uriah the Hittite, with whom King David committed adultery; she later became David's wife and the mother of King Solomon.
itens.corpo:
While her husband Uriah, an army officer, was away on campaign, David sees her bathing, sends for her, and commits adultery with her; when he learns that Bathsheba is pregnant, the king tries to cover up the deed and, failing to do so, orders that Uriah be placed at the front line of the battle to die (2 Sam 11). The prophet Nathan confronts David with the parable of the poor man's ewe lamb, leading him to acknowledge his sin publicly (2 Sam 12:1-13).

After the death of the first child born of this union, Bathsheba becomes David's lawful wife and the mother of Solomon (2 Sam 12:24). Later, as David's wife in his old age, it is she who intervenes decisively with the dying king to ensure that Solomon, and not his older brother Adonijah, would inherit the throne (1 Kings 1:11-31), thus becoming the queen mother of one of the greatest kings of Israel. Her name also appears in the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew, discreetly referred to as "the wife of Uriah" (Matt 1:6).

itens.resumo: Commander of the army of Syria, healed of leprosy by the prophet Elisha after dipping seven times in the Jordan River.
itens.corpo:
Naaman was a respected general of the Syrian army, "a great man before his master," but a leper (2 Kings 5:1). At the suggestion of a young Israelite girl, a servant of his wife who had been captured in a raid, he goes to the prophet Elisha in Israel seeking healing. Elisha, without even coming out of his house to receive him, sends a messenger to tell him only to wash seven times in the Jordan River (2 Kings 5:2-10).

Offended at not receiving a more solemn rite and at being sent to a river he considered inferior to the rivers of his own country, Naaman obeys only after the insistence of his own servants — and, when he comes up from the seventh immersion, his flesh becomes "like the flesh of a little child," completely cleansed (2 Kings 5:11-14). Naaman then acknowledges that "there is no God in all the earth, but in Israel" (2 Kings 5:15), and Elisha refuses any gift for the healing, underlining that the grace of God cannot be bought. Jesus cites this episode in the synagogue of Nazareth as an example that God's mercy extends also to foreigners (Lk 4:27).

itens.resumo: Judge of Israel who, with only three hundred men, defeats the Midianite army, trusting not in military strength but in the power of God.
itens.corpo:
At a time when the Midianites had oppressed Israel for seven years, destroying crops and flocks, an angel appears to Gideon, a humble farmer, calling him a "mighty man of valor" and sending him to deliver his people (Judg 6:11-16). Unsure of himself, Gideon asks God for confirming signs, among them the famous test of the fleece of wool, now wet and now dry, while the ground around it remained the opposite (Judg 6:36-40).

God deliberately reduces Gideon's army from thirty-two thousand to only three hundred men, "lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, 'My own hand has delivered me'" (Judg 7:2). With these three hundred men, trumpets, and jars with hidden torches, Gideon throws the Midianite camp into confusion during the night and causes it to flee in panic (Judg 7:16-22). His story, told in chapters 6 to 8 of the Book of Judges, has become a classic example that Israel's victory depends on faith in God, and not on the size of human forces.

itens.resumo: King of Persia who conquered Babylon and, by decree, allowed the exiled Jews to return and rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem.
itens.corpo:
Cyrus II ruled the Persian Empire from about 559 to 530 B.C. and, by conquering Babylon in 539 B.C., put an end to Babylonian domination over the exiled peoples, among them the Jews deported since the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. In his very first year of rule over Babylon, he issued a decree authorizing the Jews to return to their land and rebuild the Temple, even returning the sacred vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had taken (Ezra 1:1-11).

What makes Cyrus unique among biblical figures is that he is a pagan king explicitly called by God "my shepherd" and even "anointed" (mashiah) by the prophet Isaiah, about a century before his birth: "Thus says the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, [...] I call you by your name" (Is 44:28; 45:1). For the Judeo-Christian tradition, Cyrus is thus presented as an instrument of divine providence even without knowing the God of Israel, fulfilling a decisive role in the end of the Babylonian exile and in the beginning of the rebuilding of Jewish religious life.

itens.resumo: A man forced by the Roman soldiers to help Jesus carry the cross on the way to Calvary.
itens.corpo:
The three Synoptic Gospels record that, on the way to Golgotha, the Roman soldiers compelled a man who was coming in from the country, Simon, a native of Cyrene (a region of North Africa, present-day Libya), to carry the cross of Jesus (Mt 27:32; Mk 15:21; Lk 23:26). Mark adds a personal detail unusual for a minor figure: he identifies him as "the father of Alexander and Rufus" (Mk 15:21), names which suggest that Simon's two sons were known to the Christian community for which Mark was writing.

Christian tradition saw in this obligatory act, imposed by force, a living image of Jesus' call to "take up the cross" and follow him (Mt 16:24), and for this reason Simon of Cyrene became a central figure of the fifth Station of the Cross. Although nothing more is known with historical certainty about his life, some scholars associate his son Rufus with the "Rufus, chosen in the Lord," greeted by Paul in Romans 16:13, suggesting that Simon's family may have become part of the first Christian community.
